speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: Today on TuneIn, we're talking education reform. This week, the House voted on the biggest piece of legislation in 14 years regarding education. We'll talk about that right after this. Hey folks, we are back. Thanks for joining us again for another edition of TuneIn. We're talking higher education. The Every Student Succeeds Act. I shouldn't say higher education. This is K through 12. This is what affects all of us on a day-to-day basis and is the foundation for our educational experience for most of us. And that's what we're talking about. K through 12 and that hits me personally because when I have the opportunity, I actually take the kids to school. I've got a second grader and a fourth grader and I go through car line. And so I deal with this every day and my wife deals with this every day as a lot of you at home do. And I know that education is foremost and as it should be a priority, something that we want our kids to learn and grow in that K through 12 environment. And as I said, that's kind of the foundation for everything and success in life. So most everybody can tell you a story about sometimes an unpleasant experience in our public school system. And I don't say that to malign our educators because they do a fantastic job and it's a thankless job. I believe being an educator is a calling at every level and if it's not, probably need to think about getting in another line of work because I doubt anybody has ever said they're in education for the money. And that's unfortunate that that's the case, but we're dealing with in most cases some very dedicated individuals who are charged with the responsibility of teaching our children. And when I mentioned the experiences, those aren't necessarily bad experiences with the educators themselves as much as is the policy that they're forced to deal with and the confines that they have to work in. And so we're addressing that problem. And one of the problems that I heard from the first time I got elected to now is that no child left behind was in fact leaving a whole lot of children behind. And we're going to take up some legislation this week that is essentially a repeal of No Child Left Behind. It's a repeal and replace. It's been 14 years since No Child Left Behind was implemented. It's grossly out of date. I had the opportunity earlier this week to talk to Representative John Klein, who is the chairman of the Committee on Education and the Workforce. He's played a crucial role in both the House's original bill back in July and now as the conference process is taking place. Chairman Klein, thanks for being with us. I know this has been a long deal for you. You've been working on this for quite some time, certainly as long as I've been here. Can you give our folks at home and in my district a top-down view of what this education bill does?
